body.text: Prescribed expenditures are SR&ED costs that the Income Tax Regulations exclude from qualified expenditures for the federal investment tax credit. For Canadian SR&ED claimants, used depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024 may still enter the Section 37 deduction pool, but under Regulation 2902(b) it is a prescribed expenditure, reported on Form T661 Line 532, and earns no ITC.

This report provides a comprehensive technical audit and legal analysis of the Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) tax incentive regime and complementary innovation funding mechanisms in Canada as of November 2026.

Between December 2024 and November 2026, Canada enacted the most consequential structural overhaul of its R&D tax landscape since 2012. At the federal level, Bill C-15 (Budget Implementation Act), which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026, codified the measures announced in the 2024 Fall Economic Statement (December 16, 2024) and expanded in Budget 2025 (November 4, 2025). Specifically, for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, Parliament doubled the annual expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% Investment Tax Credit (ITC) from $3,000,000 to $6,000,000 (superseding the interim $4,500,000 proposal from December 2024), broadened the prior-year taxable capital phase-out thresholds from $10,000,000–$50,000,000 to $15,000,000–$75,000,000, extended access to the enhanced 35% refundable ITC to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) using a three-year average gross revenue test, and reinstated the eligibility of capital expenditures, shared-use equipment (SUE), and capital lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024. Operationally, the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) launched its optional Pre-Claim Approval Process (Form T1322) on April 1, 2026, offering eligible corporations and partnerships with under $25,000,000 in gross business income binding upfront technical eligibility determinations within eight weeks.

Concurrently, provincial jurisdictions have restructured their innovation tax architectures. Most notably, Québec's 2025–2026 Budget (tabled March 25, 2025) abolished eight legacy R&D and innovation tax credits for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, consolidating them into the unified, fully refundable Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC) (Form RD-1029.8.CR-T), which provides a 30% refundable credit on the first $1,000,000 of eligible R&D and pre-commercialization expenditures (including capital equipment) above an exclusion threshold, and 20% on the excess. Ontario automatically harmonized its Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC) and Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC) with federal capital expenditure restoration upon Royal Assent of Bill C-15 on March 26, 2026, while British Columbia made its 10% SR&ED tax credit permanent effective April 16, 2026 and aligned with the $6,000,000 limit and ECPC expansion, and Saskatchewan doubled its 10% refundable CCPC expenditure limit from $1,000,000 to $2,000,000 retroactive to December 16, 2024.
1. Federal Statutory Architecture and Legislative Evolution

Canada's federal R&D tax incentive system is governed by the Income Tax Act (R.S.C., 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.)) and Part XXIX (Sections 2900 to 2903) of the Income Tax Regulations (C.R.C., c. 945), administered jointly by the Department of Finance Canada (tax policy and legislative drafting) and the Canada Revenue Agency (technical and financial compliance). Rather than operating as a discretionary subsidy, the SR&ED Tax Incentive Program is a statutory entitlement structured around a dual-mechanism architecture: first, an immediate or indefinitely carry-forwardable income deduction via the pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures under Subsection 37(1) of the Income Tax Act; and second, a refundable and/or non-refundable Investment Tax Credit (ITC) earned on qualified SR&ED expenditures under Subsections 127(5), 127(9), 127(10.1), and 127.1(1).
1.1 The Statutory Definition of SR&ED: Subsection 248(1)

The gateway to all federal and harmonized provincial R&D tax incentives is the legal definition of "scientific research and experimental development" codified in Subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act (which was elevated from Regulation 2900 into the Act itself in 1998). Under Subsection 248(1), SR&ED means a "systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis" and that falls within one of four positive statutory branches while avoiding seven explicit statutory exclusions.
Positive Eligibility Branches: Paragraphs 248(1)(a) to (d)

items: Basic Research (Paragraph 248(1)(a)): Work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view. Basic research typically occurs in university, institutional, or foundational corporate laboratories where the objective is to discover new scientific principles, phenomena, or theoretical models without an immediate commercial deliverable.

Applied Research (Paragraph 248(1)(b)): Work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view. While basic and applied research both pursue scientific advancement by resolving scientific uncertainty, applied research directs that inquiry toward a defined commercial, medical, or industrial utility.

Experimental Development (Paragraph 248(1)(c)): Work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes, including incremental improvements thereto. Experimental development accounts for the vast majority of Canadian SR&ED claims across manufacturing, software engineering, biotechnology, clean technology, and agri-food sectors. Crucially, the statute explicitly protects incremental improvements—meaning a taxpayer does not need to invent an entirely novel product category, provided the incremental improvement requires resolving an underlying technological uncertainty that cannot be overcome through standard engineering practice.

Eligible Support Work (Paragraph 248(1)(d)): Work undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer with respect to engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, or psychological research, where the work is commensurate with the needs, and directly in support, of work described in paragraph (a), (b), or (c) that is undertaken in Canada by or on behalf of the taxpayer. This is an exhaustive, closed statutory list of eight support categories. Work in these eight categories is never eligible SR&ED on a standalone basis; it qualifies only to the extent that its scope, scale, and necessity are directly tied to and commensurate with resolving the scientific or technological uncertainty of core basic research, applied research, or experimental development carried out in Canada.

body.text: Explicit Statutory Exclusions: Paragraphs 248(1)(e) to (k)
Even where a broader corporate project involves technological innovation, Paragraphs 248(1)(e) through (k) expressly exclude seven categories of activity from the definition of SR&ED:

items: Paragraph (e): Market research or sales promotion;
Paragraph (f): Quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products, or processes;
Paragraph (g): Research in the social sciences or the humanities;
Paragraph (h): Prospecting, exploring, or drilling for, or producing, minerals, petroleum, or natural gas;
Paragraph (i): The commercial production of a new or improved material, device, or product or the commercial use of a new or improved process;
Paragraph (j): Style changes; and
Paragraph (k): Routine data collection.

body.text: As the CRA's Guidelines on the Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Tax Incentives emphasize, distinguishing between eligible support work under Paragraph 248(1)(d) (such as "testing" or "data collection") and excluded work under Paragraphs 248(1)(f) and (k) ("routine testing" or "routine data collection") turns strictly on purpose. When testing or data collection is conducted using predetermined protocols to verify compliance with established specifications or support normal commercial operations, it is excluded under Paragraphs (f) or (k). Conversely, when testing or data collection is performed specifically to validate a scientific or technological hypothesis and generate data required for basic research, applied research, or experimental development, it qualifies as eligible support work under Paragraph (d).
1.2 The Section 37 Deductible Expenditure Pool vs. Section 127 Investment Tax Credits

A frequent error in non-specialist tax literature is conflating the pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures (Subsection 37(1)) with qualified SR&ED expenditures (Subsection 127(9)). The two pools serve distinct functions and do not always contain the same dollar amounts.

The Section 37 Deductible Pool (Subsection 37(1)) accumulates allowable current SR&ED expenditures (Paragraph 37(1)(a)) and—for property acquired after December 15, 2024—allowable capital SR&ED expenditures (Paragraph 37(1)(b)) incurred in Canada related to a business carried on by the taxpayer. Under Subsection 37(1), a taxpayer may deduct any portion of the positive pool balance in the current taxation year to reduce net business income for tax purposes, or elect to leave the balance in the pool to be carried forward indefinitely to future taxation years. Because the Section 37 deduction replaces ordinary current deductions under Section 9 or Capital Cost Allowance (CCA) under Paragraph 20(1)(a), it eliminates the risk of expiring non-capital losses.

By contrast, the Section 127 Qualified Expenditure Pool (Subsection 127(9)) starts from allowable SR&ED expenditures, adds the notional Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) (Regulation 2900(4)) if the taxpayer elects the proxy method (Clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)), adds eligible Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) installments (Line 504), subtracts 20% of arm's-length SR&ED contract payments and third-party payments (leaving an 80% inclusion rate under Paragraph (a)(ii) of the definition of qualified expenditure in Subsection 127(9)), and subtracts government assistance, non-government assistance, and contract payments (Subsections 127(18) to 127(20)).

Crucially, the SR&ED deduction and the ITC are interdependent because the credit itself is taxable (Paragraph 37(1)(d) and Paragraph 12(1)(t)). Any federal SR&ED ITC claimed in a taxation year (whether applied to reduce Part I tax payable, carried back, or received as a cash refund) reduces the taxpayer's Section 37 deductible expenditure pool in the immediately following taxation year pursuant to Paragraph 37(1)(d). If the ITC reduction exceeds the available Section 37 pool balance in that subsequent year—which commonly occurs when a claimant uses the Proxy Method and deducts its entire Section 37 pool in Year 1, because the ITC earned on the notional PPA has no corresponding entry in the Section 37 pool—the negative balance is brought into taxable income in Year 2 under Paragraph 12(1)(t).
1.3 Enacted Legislative Reforms: Bill C-15 (Royal Assent March 26, 2026) and Budget 2025

Following industry consultations initiated in early 2024, the Department of Finance announced initial SR&ED enhancements in the 2024 Fall Economic Statement on December 16, 2024, which were further expanded in Budget 2025 on November 4, 2025, and enacted into law via Bill C-15, receiving Royal Assent on March 26, 2026. All core legislative amendments apply retroactively to taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024 (i.e., on or after December 16, 2024), and for capital property and lease outlays, to property acquired and available for use or lease payments first becoming payable after December 15, 2024.

body.text: 2. Federal Investment Tax Credit Rates, Thresholds, Refundability, and Carryover Mechanics

Under Subsections 127(5) and 127(9) of the Income Tax Act, the rate at which a taxpayer earns an SR&ED Investment Tax Credit and the extent to which unused credits can be refunded in cash under Section 127.1 depend on the legal classification of the claimant, its prior-year taxable capital (or three-year average gross revenue), its prior-year taxable income, and whether the underlying expenditure is of a current or capital nature.
2.1 Basic (15%) vs. Enhanced (35%) ITC Rates and Entity Classifications

The Income Tax Act establishes two primary statutory ITC rates. Under Subsection 127(9), the Basic ITC Rate is 15% of qualified SR&ED expenditures (reduced from 20% for taxation years ending after December 31, 2013). This 15% basic rate applies to foreign-controlled corporations and large Canadian public corporations that do not qualify as ECPCs, to Canadian-controlled private corporations (CCPCs) and Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) on qualified SR&ED expenditures in excess of their annual expenditure limit, and to sole proprietorships (individuals), beneficiaries of trusts, and members of partnerships.

Under Subsection 127(10.1), an additional 20% credit rate is added to the 15% basic rate—yielding an Enhanced ITC Rate of 35%—on qualified SR&ED expenditures up to the taxpayer's annual expenditure limit (Subsection 127(10.2)). For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, both CCPCs and ECPCs earn the 35% enhanced rate up to the $6,000,000 annual expenditure limit (shared among associated corporations under Subsection 127(10.21) via Schedule T2SCH49 or among consolidated group members for ECPCs).
2.2 Comprehensive Refundability Matrix by Claimant Category

When a claimant has no federal Part I tax payable (or after reducing Part I tax payable to zero), Section 127.1 governs whether the remaining unclaimed ITC balance is paid out as a cash refund. The CRA's SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy (updated October 7, 2026) distinguishes between corporate and non-corporate profiles based on the definitions of qualifying corporation and excluded corporation in Subsection 127.1(2).

A Qualifying Corporation (Subsection 127.1(2)) is defined as a CCPC throughout the taxation year (and any associated corporations) whose taxable income for the immediately preceding taxation year did not exceed its qualifying income limit. For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, the qualifying income limit formula is:

In this formula, A is nil if the prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada of the CCPC (and associated corporations) is below the $15,000,000 threshold, or the amount by which prior-year taxable capital exceeds the threshold up to $60,000,000. (For taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024, the denominator and cap were $40,000,000 above a $10,000,000 threshold). Conversely, an Excluded Corporation (Subsection 127.1(2)) is a corporation that is controlled by, or related to, one or more persons exempt from Part I tax under Section 149, Her Majesty in right of a province, a Canadian municipality, or any other public authority.

body.text: A critical statutory restriction applies to partnerships under Subsection 127(8) and the Tax Court of Canada precedent in All Colour Chemicals Ltd. v. The Queen. Because a partnership is not a "person" or a "CCPC" for income tax purposes, SR&ED ITCs computed at the partnership level are calculated strictly at the 15% basic rate and allocated to active general partners (Subsection 127(8)). As established in All Colour Chemicals, a corporate partner that is a CCPC cannot claim the 35% enhanced rate on partnership-allocated SR&ED expenditures because Subsection 127(8) overrides Subsection 127(10.1). Furthermore, under Subsection 127(8.1), specified members of a partnership (including all limited partners and passive general partners) are strictly prohibited from receiving any allocation of SR&ED ITCs; any unallocated ITCs attributable to specified members are reallocated to active general partners (who may elect to renounce them via Form T932 under Subsection 127(8.4)).
2.3 Expenditure Limit Phase-Out Methodologies (Taxable Capital vs. Three-Year Gross Revenue)
For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, the $6,000,000 annual expenditure limit under Subsection 127(10.2) is reduced gradually under two statutory methodologies:

items: Taxable Capital Employed in Canada Method (Default for CCPCs): For a CCPC (and its associated group across their last taxation years ending in the preceding calendar year), the expenditure limit remains at the full $6,000,000 until combined taxable capital employed in Canada reaches $15,000,000. Once prior-year taxable capital reaches $15,000,000, the $6,000,000 expenditure limit decreases gradually and becomes nil when prior-year taxable capital reaches $75,000,000: Expenditure Limit = $6,000,000 × [($75,000,000 − Prior-Year Taxable Capital Employed in Canada) ÷ $60,000,000]

Three-Year Average Annual Gross Revenue Method (Mandatory for ECPCs; Elective for CCPCs): Because public corporations frequently raise substantial equity capital on public markets before generating commercial revenue, applying a taxable capital test would prematurely disqualify R&D-intensive public issuers. Accordingly, for Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs)—specifically small- and medium-sized Canadian public corporations with less than $75,000,000 in gross revenue on average over the preceding three years—the expenditure limit gradual reduction is calculated using the average annual revenue reflected in the financial statements over the preceding three fiscal years across all members of the consolidated group, regardless of whether corporations were associated during the entirety of that three-year period. Under Section 3.1 of the CRA's SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy, CCPCs may also elect to use this three-year average annual revenue method in lieu of the taxable capital method by filing the prescribed form.

Short Taxation Years (Section 3.1.2, CRA ITC Policy): If a corporation has a taxation year of fewer than 365 days (for example, due to incorporation, amalgamation, or an acquisition of control), the calculated expenditure limit is prorated based on the number of days in the taxation year relative to 365.

body.text: 2.4 Carryback, Carryforward, and Acquisition of Control Rules

When an SR&ED ITC is non-refundable (or when a claimant elects not to claim a refund), Subsection 127(5) and the definition of investment tax credit in Subsection 127(9) govern carryover periods. Unused ITCs earned in the current taxation year may be carried back up to 3 preceding taxation years to reduce federal Part I tax otherwise payable in those prior years (limited to the current-year ITC in excess of the amount needed to reduce current-year Part I tax to nil), or carried forward for up to 20 subsequent taxation years to offset future Part I tax payable. Any credit not utilized within the 20-year carryforward window expires. As confirmed by the Tax Court of Canada in Ainsworth Lumber Co. v. The Queen, Subsection 127(5) uses permissive language ("may"), allowing a taxpayer to elect the order in which it applies refundable versus non-refundable credits against Part I tax.

Upon an acquisition of control of a corporation (or a trust acquiring a new majority-interest beneficiary), a deemed year-end occurs and both the undeducted Section 37 SR&ED expenditure pool and unused pre-acquisition ITC carryforwards are subject to loss restriction streaming rules. Under the CRA's Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures Policy, the pre-acquisition Section 37 pool is reduced to nil unless the exact business to which the SR&ED expenditures related continues to be carried on for profit or with a reasonable expectation of profit, and deductions in subsequent years are limited strictly to income derived from that same business or a similar business. Similarly, an acquisition of control restricts the ability to carry forward pre-acquisition unused ITCs or carry back post-acquisition unused ITCs.
3. Qualifying Expenditures (QREs) and Overhead Calculation Methodologies

Once technical eligibility is established under Subsection 248(1), expenditures must be classified, tracked, and quantified in accordance with Section 37, Subsection 127(9), and Regulations 2900 and 2902.
3.1 Traditional Method vs. Proxy Method (Clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A) vs. (B))

Every SR&ED claimant must elect on Form T661 (Lines 160 and 162) between two mutually exclusive calculation methods for each taxation year: the Proxy Method (Clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)) or the Traditional Method (Clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)). Under Subsection 37(10), this election must be made when Form T661 is first filed for the taxation year and is irrevocable for that taxation year; if no election is made on Form T661, the Traditional Method applies automatically by default.

Under the Proxy Method (Clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B) and Regulation 2900(4)), the claimant does not specifically track or include actual SR&ED overhead and other expenditures on Form T661. Instead, the claimant calculates a notional Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) equal to 55% of the salary base of employees directly engaged in SR&ED in Canada. It is vital to verify that the statutory PPA rate under Subsection 2900(4) of the Income Tax Regulations has been 55% since 2014 (having declined from 65% in 2012 and 60% in 2013); any claim that the proxy rate is 65% or 60% for current filings is erroneous. The 55% PPA is reported on Line 502 of Form T661 (calculated in Part 5, Line 820) solely to increase qualified SR&ED expenditures for calculating the SR&ED ITC. The PPA is not added to the Section 37 pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures; instead, the actual overhead expenses represented by the PPA (such as office supplies, heat, water, electricity, telephones, support staff wages, travel, training, property taxes, and maintenance) remain deductible as ordinary business expenses under Section 9.

Under the Traditional Method (Clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A) and Regulations 2900(2) & 2900(3)), the claimant specifically identifies, tracks, and substantiates actual overhead and other current expenditures on Line 360 of Form T661 that are either all or substantially all (ASA, ≥90%) attributable or directly attributable (meaning directly related and incremental—would not have been incurred had the SR&ED not occurred) to the prosecution of SR&ED or the provision of premises, facilities, or equipment for SR&ED in Canada. Under the Traditional Method, actual allowable overhead is included in both the Section 37 deductible pool and the Section 127(9) qualified expenditure pool for ITC purposes.

body.text: 3.2 Salaries and Wages: Specified Employees, YMPE Caps, and the 180-Day Unpaid Rule

Salaries and wages (Subsection 248(1), income from an office or employment under Sections 5 to 8, reported on T4 slips) form the core expenditure category in most Canadian SR&ED claims. Self-employed drawings or partnership distributions paid to sole proprietors or partners are not salaries or wages from employment and cannot be claimed. Similarly, stock option benefits (Section 7 and Section 143.3), retiring allowances, extended vacation or sick leave, and the employer's share of payroll benefits (CPP, QPP, EI, WSIB, CNESST) are excluded from SR&ED salaries and wages.
Specified Employees and Dual Statutory Caps (Subsection 37(9) vs. Regulation 2900(7))

A specified employee (Subsection 248(1)) is an employee who is a specified shareholder of the employer—defined as a person who owns, directly or indirectly, at any time in the year, 10% or more of the issued shares of any class of the corporation or a related corporation (including shares owned by persons with whom the employee does not deal at arm's length)—or who is related to a specified shareholder (such as a spouse, sibling, or child). To prevent owner-managers from inflating refundable ITCs through year-end bonus declarations, the Income Tax Act and Income Tax Regulations impose three distinct limitations on specified employees:

items: Absolute Prohibition on Bonuses and Profit-Based Remuneration (Subsection 37(9)): While bonuses and remuneration based on profits paid to non-specified (arm's-length) employees are allowable SR&ED salary expenditures on Line 300 (though still excluded from the Proxy Salary Base on Line 812 under Regulation 2900(9)), a specified employee's bonuses and remuneration based on profits are strictly disallowed from both the Section 37 pool and the Section 127 ITC calculation.

Cap 1 — Maximum Allowable Direct SR&ED Salary Pool (Subsection 37(9.1)): The maximum amount of base salary or wages of a specified employee that can be claimed as an allowable SR&ED expenditure on Form T661 Line 305 (under either the Traditional or Proxy Method) is capped at 5 times the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) determined under Section 18 of the Canada Pension Plan for the calendar year in which the taxation year ends, prorated by the number of days the individual was employed in the taxation year: Maximum Specified Employee SR&ED Salary (Line 305) = 5 × YMPE × (Days Employed in the Taxation Year ÷ 365) If a specified employee performs SR&ED for two or more associated corporations, the 5 × YMPE cap must be shared and allocated among the associated corporations using Form T1174 (Agreement Between Associated Corporations to Allocate Salary or Wages of Specified Employees for SR&ED), filed on or before the corporations' respective SR&ED reporting deadlines. Failure to file Form T1174 deems the specified employee's SR&ED salary to be nil.

Cap 2 — Maximum Proxy Salary Base Inclusion (Subsections 2900(7), 2900(8), and 2900(10)): When calculating the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) in Part 5 of Form T661 (Lines 850 to 860), a second, tighter ceiling restricts the salary base for each specified employee (after already excluding bonuses, profit-based pay, taxable benefits under Section 6, stock options under Section 7, and prior-year unpaid wages under Subsection 78(4)). Under Subsection 2900(7), the amount included in the proxy salary base (Line 860) for a specified employee cannot exceed the lesser of:

The specified employee's eligible salary or wages multiplied by the percentage of time spent directly engaged in SR&ED (Line 856), where the time percentage (Line 854) is capped at 75% of total working time (Regulation 2900(7)(a)—meaning that even if a founder spends 100% of their time hands-on in SR&ED, at most 75% of their total eligible salary can enter the proxy salary base); or

2.5 × YMPE prorated by the number of days employed in the taxation year (Regulation 2900(7)(b), Line 858: 2.5 × YMPE × (Days Employed ÷ 365)), shared across associated corporations and related individuals/partnerships (Regulations 2900(8) and 2900(10)).

body.text: The All-or-Substantially-All (ASA) 90% Rule, Foreign Work Cap (10%), and 180-Day Unpaid Rules

Under Regulation 2900(5) and the CRA's SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy, if an employee (subject to subsections 2900(6) to (8) for specified employees) spends all or substantially all (ASA, defined as 90% or more) of their working time throughout the taxation year directly engaged in SR&ED in Canada, 100% of their eligible salary or wages is included in allowable SR&ED wages and in the proxy salary base.

For permissible SR&ED work performed outside Canada (Form T661 Lines 307 and 309), salaries or wages paid to Canadian-resident employees qualify only if the foreign work was solely in support of SR&ED carried on in Canada, the remuneration was not subject to income or profits tax in the foreign country, and the total foreign SR&ED wages across all employees do not exceed 10% of the total SR&ED salaries and wages for work performed in Canada (Form T661 Line 306).

Strict statutory timing rules govern accrued but unpaid expenses at year-end. Under Subsection 78(4), any salary or wages incurred in a taxation year that remain unpaid 180 days after the end of the taxation year are deemed not to have been incurred in that year (Form T661 Line 315), and instead are deemed incurred in the subsequent taxation year in which they are actually paid (Form T661 Line 310). Even when paid in a subsequent year and claimed on Line 310, Paragraph 2900(9)(b) permanently excludes prior-year unpaid wages from the Proxy Salary Base. Similarly, under Subsection 127(26), current expenditures other than salaries or wages (such as contractor or material payables) that remain unpaid 180 days after the end of the taxation year (Form T661 Line 520) are excluded from qualified expenditures for ITC purposes until the taxation year in which they are actually paid (Form T661 Line 500).
3.3 Overall Cap on the Prescribed Proxy Amount (Regulation 2900(6))

To ensure that total qualified SR&ED expenditures, the PPA, and specified statutory deductions do not exceed the total business expenditures deducted by the claimant in the year, Subsection 2900(6) of the Income Tax Regulations subjects the calculated PPA to an Overall Cap:
Maximum PPA = A − B − C

In this statutory formula, A is the total of all amounts deducted in computing the taxpayer's net income for tax purposes from the business for the year (including Cost of Goods Sold; if a claimant carries on more than one business, deductions across all businesses are summed). Variable B is the total of all deductions claimed in the year under Section 20 (such as Capital Cost Allowance [CCA], interest, and bad debts), Section 24 (ceasing to carry on a business), Section 26 (banks), Section 30 (improving land for farming), Section 32 (insurance agents or brokers), Section 37 (the SR&ED deduction claimed on Line 411 of Schedule T2SCH1), Sections 66 to 66.8 (exploration and development expenses), and Section 104 (trusts). Variable C is the total amount incurred by the taxpayer in the year for the use of, or the right to use, a building (other than a special-purpose building prescribed under Regulation 2903). As the CRA's Prescribed Proxy Amount Policy notes, the Overall Cap will not restrict the PPA provided the claimant has deducted more than $55 of non-SR&ED operating expenses (excluding items in B and C) for every $100 of eligible salary in the salary base.
3.4 Materials Consumed vs. Materials Transformed and Recapture (Subsections 127(27)–(35))

Under Paragraph 2900(2)(a) and Subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(V) (and the CRA's Materials for SR&ED Policy), the cost of materials is an allowable current SR&ED expenditure under both the Traditional and Proxy Methods if the items compose the body of a thing on which SR&ED is being performed in Canada and are either consumed or transformed.

Materials Consumed (Form T661 Line 320) are materials that are absorbed, used up, destroyed, or rendered virtually valueless (retaining less than 10% of their original cost) as a result of SR&ED. Under the CRA's 90% Rule, if 90% or more of the value of a material is consumed in SR&ED, 100% of its cost is allowable as a consumed material expenditure. Items that do not compose the body of the object being worked on—such as broken lab supplies, cleaning supplies, CDs/DVDs, and engine lubricants—do not qualify as materials (though they may qualify as overhead on Line 360 under the Traditional Method). Similarly, general utilities (electricity, fuel, boiler feed water, floor-washing water) are overhead, whereas process water that becomes part of intermediate/final experimental products and direct energy inputs in endothermic chemical, petrochemical, pharmaceutical, biotechnology, metallurgical, cement, glass, ceramics, and plastics-forming processes qualify as materials consumed.

Materials Transformed (Form T661 Line 325) are materials changed or incorporated into another material, prototype, or experimental production during SR&ED that retain some commercial or scrap value (more than 10% of original cost). Under the SR&ED During Production Runs Policy and SR&ED While Developing an Asset Policy, constructing duplicate copies of a prototype strictly for testing in support of SR&ED qualifies as materials for SR&ED when the tests are completed, and experimental development during production runs is evaluated under either the ED+EP (Experimental Development resulting in Experimental Production) or ED+CP (Experimental Development Simultaneous with Commercial Production, where only incremental costs qualify) framework.

However, if property that incorporates materials transformed (or property acquired via an SR&ED contract or capital/SUE expenditure) on which a federal SR&ED ITC was earned in any of the 20 preceding taxation years is subsequently sold or converted to commercial use, Subsections 127(27) to 127(35) trigger ITC Recapture. The recaptured credit (computed at the 35% or 15% rate originally earned, multiplied by the proceeds of disposition or fair market value at conversion, capped at the original ITC) is added directly to Part I tax payable for the year of sale or conversion, and simultaneously increases the claimant's Section 37 deductible SR&ED expenditure pool for the following taxation year.
3.5 Subcontractors, Non-Arm's Length Contracts, and Third-Party Payments

When a claimant contracts an arm's-length taxable supplier in Canada to perform SR&ED on its behalf (Subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.01) & Form T661 Line 340), 100% of the eligible current contract expenditure enters the Section 37 deductible pool, while 80% counts as a qualified SR&ED expenditure for calculating the ITC (Paragraph (a)(ii) of qualified expenditure in Subsection 127(9); the 20% reduction is entered on Form T661 Line 529). Under the CRA's Contract Expenditures for SR&ED Performed on Behalf of a Claimant Policy, "on behalf of" requires that the payer typically maintains ownership of the SR&ED work and bears the technical and financial risk. Placement agency workers are treated as contractors (80% ITC inclusion), and if an arm's-length contractor is hired to perform only support work (Paragraph 248(1)(d)), the payer can claim 80% of the contract cost even though the contractor cannot claim SR&ED in its own right. Under the Look-Through Rule, the payer's contract expenditure must exclude any non-current expenditure of the performer, and the performer must notify the payer in writing within 90 days after calendar year-end.

By contrast, if a claimant enters into an SR&ED contract with a non-arm's length (NAL) party (Subsections 127(13) to 127(16)), the payer's contract expenditure is deductible in its Section 37 pool but earns 0% ITC directly. Instead, the NAL performer claims its own SR&ED expenditures (which are not reduced by the inter-company payment) and may transfer all or part of its qualified expenditures (up to the contract price) to the payer by filing Form T1146 (Agreement to Transfer Qualified Expenditures Incurred in Respect of SR&ED Contracts Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length, reported on Line 508 / Line 510). Furthermore, when a claimant purchases goods, property, or non-SR&ED services from a NAL party, Subsections 127(11.6) to 127(11.8) cap the qualified expenditure at the NAL supplier's adjusted selling cost or adjusted service cost, eliminating inter-company profit.

Finally, Third-Party Payments (Subparagraphs 37(1)(a)(i.1), (ii), and (iii), Form T1263, and Form T661 Line 370) are payments made to approved associations (B entities), approved universities, affiliated colleges, or research institutes (C entities), tax-exempt non-profit SR&ED corporations under Paragraph 149(1)(j) (D and F entities), approved granting councils such as NSERC, CIHR, and SSHRC (E entities), or Canadian-resident corporations (A entities), where the claimant is entitled to exploit the results of the SR&ED in Canada. Like arm's-length subcontracts, third-party payments are 100% deductible in the Section 37 pool and 80% eligible for the SR&ED ITC (20% subtracted on Line 529).
3.6 Reinstated Capital Expenditures, Shared-Use Equipment (SUE), Lease Costs, and Cloud/Software Rules (Post-December 15, 2024)

Enacted by Bill C-15 on March 26, 2026, the restoration of SR&ED capital expenditures, Shared-Use Equipment (SUE), and lease costs applies to depreciable property acquired (and available for use) or lease payments first becoming payable after December 15, 2024. Capital expenditures or lease payments incurred after December 31, 2013 and before December 16, 2024 remain strictly ineligible.

items: SR&ED Capital Expenditures (Paragraph 37(1)(b) & Form T661 Line 390 — CRA Policy updated June 29, 2026): Covers depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024 where the claimant intends at the time of acquisition either to use the property for all or substantially all (ASA, ≥90%) of its operating time over its expected useful life for SR&ED in Canada (Operating Time Test) or to consume ASA (≥90%) of its value in SR&ED in Canada (Value Consumption Test). Land (non-depreciable) and buildings or leasehold interests in buildings are excluded (Paragraph 37(8)(d)), other than prescribed special-purpose buildings under Regulation 2903. Used depreciable property may enter the Section 37 pool but is a prescribed expenditure under Regulation 2902(b) (Form T661 Line 532) and is ineligible for the ITC. Claimants report ASA capital expenditures on Line 390 (and list the 10 most expensive properties per project on Lines 262 and 263). For a CCPC or ECPC, the 35% ITC earned on capital expenditures is 40% refundable.

Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) (Subsection 127(9) & Form T661 Line 504 — CRA Policy updated May 22, 2026): Covers new depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024 that does not meet the ≥90% ASA test, is not General Purpose Office Equipment or Furniture (GPOEF), and is not Prescribed Depreciable Property (PDP) under Subsection 2900(11) (property intended at acquisition to be used during commercial facility assembly/commissioning and thereafter primarily for commercial purposes). If used primarily (more than 50% and less than 90% of operating time) for SR&ED in Canada, SUE earns an ITC on 25% of its capital cost in the First Period (First-Term SUE, ending at the first tax year-end at least 12 months after acquisition) and an additional 25% of its capital cost in the Second Period (Second-Term SUE, ending at the first tax year-end at least 24 months after acquisition), up to 50% in total on Line 504. SUE is depreciated via regular CCA on Schedule T2SCH8 rather than entering the Section 37 pool, and the ITC reduces the CCA class UCC in the subsequent year.

Equipment Lease Costs (SR&ED Lease Expenditures Policy, updated June 8, 2026): For lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024, building rent remains excluded (unless a prescribed special-purpose building). Under the Traditional Method, if leased equipment (including GPOEF) is used ASA (≥90%) in SR&ED, 100% of the lease cost is claimed as a lease expenditure; if used less than 90%, the proportional SR&ED operating-time percentage is claimed as overhead on Line 360 (provided it is directly related and incremental). Under the Proxy Method, leased GPOEF and land are completely excluded (covered by the 55% PPA); for other leased equipment, 100% of the lease cost is claimable if used ASA (≥90%), 50% of the lease cost is claimable if used primarily (>50% to <90%), and 0% is claimable if used 50% or less.

Software Licenses vs. Cloud Computing / SaaS Subscriptions: Under the CRA's SR&ED Capital Expenditures Policy (June 29, 2026), computer software or licenses used as a tool for conducting SR&ED (e.g., CAD or simulation software, excluding software incorporated into a commercial product for sale) that provide an enduring benefit lasting beyond one year are capital expenditures (eligible if acquired after December 15, 2024). Conversely, cloud computing instances, SaaS subscriptions, and annual/monthly CAD subscriptions that benefit only the current period are current overhead expenditures. Therefore, a claimant using the Proxy Method cannot claim cloud or SaaS subscriptions separately because all overhead is already represented by the 55% PPA (Regulation 2900(4)); claiming them under the Proxy Method constitutes impermissible double-counting. Only claimants electing the Traditional Method can claim incremental, directly related cloud/SaaS costs on Line 360.

body.text: 4. Government Assistance, Contract Payments, and Federal-Provincial Stacking Mechanics

Under Paragraph 37(1)(c) and Subsections 127(18), 127(19), and 127(20) of the Income Tax Act, a claimant must reduce its SR&ED pools by any government assistance, non-government assistance, or contract payments that it has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive on or before the filing-due date of its income tax return for the taxation year.
4.1 Government Assistance, Non-Government Assistance, and Contract Payments (Subsection 127(9))

Government Assistance (Subsection 127(9)) encompasses any grant, subsidy, forgivable loan, deduction from tax, provincial or territorial R&D tax credit, or investment allowance from a government, municipality, Crown corporation, foreign government, or public authority, other than the federal SR&ED ITC itself. This includes federal grants such as the NRC Industrial Research Assistance Program (IRAP), wage subsidies (such as CEWS/TWS in prior years), and all provincial and territorial R&D tax credits. Non-Government Assistance includes any inducement, reimbursement, or contribution that would be included in income under Paragraph 12(1)(x). Contract Payments are amounts payable by an arm's-length taxable supplier—or by a Canadian government, municipality, public authority, or tax-exempt entity (Section 149)—for SR&ED performed for it or on its behalf. (In Com Dev Ltd. v. The Queen, the Tax Court held that a fixed-price commercial contract for the sale of a finished good where the vendor bears the financial risk is commercial revenue rather than a "contract payment" for SR&ED).

Reductions are applied on a project-by-project basis (Subsections 127(18)–(20)); if assistance or contract payments on a project exceed the recipient's qualified expenditures on that project, the excess carries forward to reduce future qualified expenditures on that project and, in non-arm's length groups, must be allocated among NAL group members working on the project via Form T1145 (Subsection 127(20)). Additionally, following the reinstatement of SR&ED capital expenditures, Department of Finance legislative amendments (including Section 127.491 for the Clean Electricity ITC, effective May 4, 2026, alongside the Clean Technology, Clean Hydrogen, and Clean Technology Manufacturing ITC provisions) strictly prohibit claiming both an SR&ED ITC and a federal Clean Economy ITC on the same capital expenditure.
4.2 Mathematical Walkthrough: Federal + Provincial Credit Stacking and the PPA Assistance Rule

To demonstrate the exact statutory mechanics under the Proxy Method, consider a qualifying Canadian-controlled private corporation (CCPC) with a permanent establishment in Ontario (claiming the 8% refundable OITC and 3.5% non-refundable ORDTC) during a taxation year beginning January 1, 2026 (post-Bill C-15 regime), with the following R&D transactions:

items: Direct Hands-On SR&ED Salaries (4 arm's-length engineers, 100% SR&ED time, Line 300): $1,000,000
Materials Consumed in SR&ED (Line 320): $100,000
Arm's-Length Canadian SR&ED Subcontractor (Line 340): $200,000
New SR&ED Testing Equipment Acquired February 2026 (Used 100% ASA for SR&ED, Line 390): $300,000
NRC IRAP Grant Received for Engineer Salaries (Line 515): $150,000

body.text: Step-by-Step Computation of Allowable, Qualified, Provincial, and Federal Amounts

items: Allowable SR&ED Expenditures (Form T661 Part 3): Allowable current expenditures (Line 380) equal $1,000,000 (Wages) + $100,000 (Materials) + $200,000 (Subcontracts) = $1,300,000. Adding allowable capital expenditures (Line 390) of $300,000 yields Total Allowable SR&ED Expenditures (Line 400) of $1,600,000.

Prescribed Proxy Amount (Form T661 Part 5, Line 820 & Line 502): Because all $1,000,000 of direct SR&ED wages were paid to arm's-length employees with no bonuses or taxable benefits, the Salary Base is $1,000,000, generating a 55% PPA of $550,000 (Regulation 2900(4)).

Pre-Assistance Qualified Expenditures (Form T661 Part 4): Applying the 20% statutory reduction (Line 529 = -$40,000) to the $200,000 arm's-length subcontract leaves $160,000 (80%). Pre-assistance qualified expenditures therefore total $1,000,000 (Wages) + $550,000 (PPA) + $100,000 (Materials) + $160,000 (80% Subcontract) + $300,000 (Capital) = $2,110,000 (comprising $1,810,000 current/PPA and $300,000 capital). Subtracting the $150,000 NRC IRAP grant (Line 515) leaves $1,960,000 ($1,660,000 current/PPA and $300,000 capital) as the eligible base for Ontario R&D tax credits.

Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC — Schedule 566, 8% Refundable): Because Ontario automatically harmonized with Bill C-15 to include 100% of post-December 15, 2024 qualified capital expenditures, the entire $1,960,000 base qualifies (within the $3,000,000 OITC cap), generating an 8% refundable OITC of $156,800 ($132,800 on current/PPA and $24,000 on capital).

Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC — Schedule 508, 3.5% Non-Refundable): Under Ontario law, the $156,800 OITC reduces the eligible expenditure base for the ORDTC to $1,960,000 − $156,800 = $1,803,200 ($1,527,200 current/PPA and $276,000 capital), generating a 3.5% non-refundable ORDTC of $63,112 ($53,452 on current/PPA and $9,660 on capital). Total Ontario provincial assistance (Line 513) is $156,800 + $63,112 = $219,912.

Federal Qualified SR&ED Expenditures (Line 570) and Enhanced 35% ITC (Schedule T2SCH31): Subtracting the $219,912 of Ontario tax credits from the $1,960,000 post-IRAP base yields Total Federal Qualified SR&ED Expenditures (Line 570) of $1,740,088, consisting of $1,473,748 of net current/PPA expenditures and $266,340 of net capital expenditures. Because the entire $1,740,088 is within the CCPC's $6,000,000 expenditure limit, it earns the 35% enhanced ITC:
Federal ITC on Current & PPA Spend (100% Refundable): 35% × $1,473,748 = $515,811.80.
Federal ITC on Capital Spend (40% Refundable / 60% Non-Refundable): 35% × $266,340 = $93,219.00, of which 40% ($37,287.60) is refundable in cash and 60% ($55,931.40) is non-refundable.
Total Federal SR&ED ITC Earned: $515,811.80 + $93,219.00 = $609,030.80.

Combined Recovery & PPA Assistance Pool Rule (Section 4.3.1, CRA Assistance Policy): Across the $1,600,000 of actual cash R&D outlay, the corporation secures $978,942.80 in total funding and tax credits (61.18% of outlay), including $859,899.40 in immediate cash ($150,000 IRAP + $156,800 OITC + $515,811.80 federal current ITC + $37,287.60 federal capital ITC refund) and $119,043.40 in non-refundable credit carryforwards ($63,112 ORDTC + $55,931.40 non-refundable federal capital ITC). Furthermore, under Section 4.3.1 of the CRA's Assistance and Contract Payments Policy, the portion of the Ontario OITC and ORDTC attributable to the notional $550,000 PPA ($61,710) does not reduce the Section 37 deductible expenditure pool (since the PPA is not in the Section 37 pool), but instead is included directly in income in the year received under Paragraph 12(1)(x).

body.text: 5. Provincial and Territorial R&D Tax Credit Regimes

Nine Canadian provinces and one territory (Yukon) provide statutory R&D tax credits that stack with the federal SR&ED program, while three jurisdictions—Prince Edward Island, the Northwest Territories, and Nunavut—do not offer a provincial or territorial R&D tax credit. Except for Québec (administered by Revenu Québec via the CO-17 return) and Alberta (administered by Alberta Tax and Revenue Administration [TRA] via the AT1 return), all provincial and territorial R&D tax credits are administered directly by the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) through the federal T2 Corporation Income Tax Return (Schedule 5).
5.1 Québec: The 2025/2026 CRIC Consolidation and Innovation Regime

In the Québec 2025–2026 Budget tabled on March 25, 2025 (Information Bulletin 2025-6), the Québec Ministry of Finance enacted a landmark overhaul of its provincial R&D tax architecture. For taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, Québec abolished eight legacy R&D and innovation tax measures and replaced them with a single, harmonized, fully refundable credit: the Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC) (Crédit d'impôt pour la recherche, l'innovation et la commercialisation).
The Eight Legacy Québec Tax Measures Abolished and Replaced by CRIC (Tax Years Beginning After March 25, 2025)
Any reference in older literature to Québec's former 14% to 30% fragmented R&D credits applies only to taxation years that began on or before March 25, 2025. The eight replaced programs are:

items: R&D Tax Credit for Salaries and Wages (Crédit d'impôt relatif aux salaires – R-D, formerly 30% for SMEs and 14% for large businesses, with $50,000 to $225,000 exclusion thresholds);
R&D Tax Credit for University Research or Public Research Centres (formerly 30% for SMEs and 14% for large businesses on 80% of an eligible R&D contract);
R&D Tax Credit for Private Partnership Pre-Competitive Research (formerly 30% for SMEs and 14% for large businesses on 100% of current spend and 80% of subcontracts);
R&D Tax Credit for Fees and Dues Paid to a Research Consortium (formerly 30% for SMEs and 14% for large businesses on 100% of contributions);
Tax Credit for Industrial Design (formerly 24% for SMEs and 12% for large businesses);
Tax Credit for Technology Adaptation Services (formerly 40% on 80% of fees paid to a CCTT or CLT);
Tax Holiday for Foreign Researchers (formerly a 5-year sliding 100%/75%/50%/25% personal income tax exemption); and
Tax Holiday for Foreign Experts (formerly a 5-year sliding 100%/75%/50%/25% personal income tax exemption).

body.text: Statutory Parameters of the New Québec CRIC (Tax Years Beginning After March 25, 2025)

Unlike the legacy regime, CRIC eliminates company-size distinctions between SMEs and large or foreign-controlled corporations. Every eligible corporation operating a business with an establishment in Québec earns a 100% refundable tax credit equal to 30% on the first $1,000,000 of qualified expenditures above the applicable exclusion threshold (shared among associated corporations via Form RD-1029.8.EN-T), and 20% on all qualified expenditures exceeding the $1,000,000 limit, with no upper ceiling.

Crucially, CRIC covers both R&D activities (harmonized with the federal Subsection 248(1) definition of basic research, applied research, experimental development, and support work, with scientific review conducted by the CRA) and Pre-Commercialization Activities (Form RD-1029.8.PR-T) undertaken in Québec as a continuation of R&D carried out in Québec by or on behalf of the corporation. Eligible pre-commercialization activities include: (1) tests, technological validations, and studies conducted to satisfy regulatory requirements and obtain an initial approval or certification for commercializing an innovation; (2) product design, including form and aesthetics development, functional improvements, and choice of materials; and (3) quality control activities strictly related to implementing a quality control system required for initial regulatory approval or certification.

Qualified expenditures under CRIC comprise 100% of salaries and wages paid to employees for eligible R&D or pre-commercialization work in Québec, 50% of amounts paid to subcontractors for contracts carried out in Québec, 50% of payments made to eligible public research centres, research consortia, or university entities in Québec, and 100% of capital property acquisition costs (CAPEX) acquired to perform eligible R&D or pre-commercialization in Québec (excluding land, buildings, rights to use land or buildings, and property covered by a Large Investment Project tax holiday). Before applying the 30% and 20% credit rates, qualified expenditures for the taxation year must exceed an Applicable Exclusion Threshold equal to the greater of $50,000 or the sum of the Québec basic personal amount under the personal income tax system (e.g., $18,571 in 2025) for each eligible employee, prorated by the percentage of time each employee devoted to eligible R&D and pre-commercialization activities. Corporations claim CRIC by filing Form RD-1029.8.CR-T (Codes 112 and 113)—alongside Form RD-222 for the Québec R&D income deduction—with their CO-17 return within 18 months of fiscal year-end. Dual claiming of CRIC and another Québec credit (such as the C3i investment and innovation credit) on the same expenditure is prohibited.

Québec also operates two major complementary innovation regimes: first, for taxation years beginning after December 31, 2025, Québec replaced the former E-Business Tax Credit (CDAE) with the CDAE-IA (AI Adoption Tax Credit), providing a 30% refundable credit (subject to Investissement Québec attestation) for IT corporations with at least six eligible employees that integrate artificial intelligence (AI) into high-value digital solutions; and second, the Incentive Deduction for the Commercialization of Innovations (DICI) patent box reduces the effective Québec corporate tax rate from 11.5% to 2.0% (a 17.0% combined federal-Québec tax rate) on eligible income from commercializing qualified Québec-developed patents, certificates of supplementary protection, or copyrighted software.
5.2 Ontario: OITC, ORDTC, and OBRITC

Ontario administers three distinct corporate R&D tax credits under the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario) via the federal T2 return. Following Royal Assent of federal Bill C-15 on March 26, 2026, Ontario automatically restored the eligibility of 100% of qualified capital expenditures acquired on or after December 16, 2024 for both the OITC and the ORDTC.

The Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC — Section 96, Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario) — Schedule 566 [T2SCH566]) provides an 8% fully refundable tax credit on qualified Ontario SR&ED expenditures (100% of current expenditures and 100% of post-December 15, 2024 capital expenditures) up to a $3,000,000 annual expenditure limit (a maximum annual refundable credit of $240,000), shared among associated corporations. The $3,000,000 expenditure limit phases out linearly if prior-year federal taxable income of the corporation (and associated group) is between $500,000 and $800,000, or if prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada is between $25,000,000 and $50,000,000.

The Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC — Section 38, Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario) — Schedule 508 [T2SCH508]) provides a 3.5% non-refundable tax credit on all eligible Ontario SR&ED expenditures (100% of current and post-December 15, 2024 capital spend), with no expenditure limit and no size phase-out. Any OITC claimed reduces the eligible expenditure base for the ORDTC. Unused ORDTC carries back 3 years and carries forward 20 years against Ontario corporate income tax, and a corporation may deliver a written waiver of the ORDTC within 6 months of tax year-end (or on an amended return) to avoid reducing its federal SR&ED qualified expenditure pool when in a loss position.

The Ontario Business-Research Institute Tax Credit (OBRITC — Section 97, Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario) — Schedules 568 & 569 [T2SCH568, T2SCH569]) provides a 20% fully refundable tax credit on qualified current SR&ED expenditures incurred in Ontario under an eligible contract with an Eligible Research Institute (ERI) (Ontario universities, community colleges, hospital research institutes, or Ontario Centres of Excellence), capped at $20,000,000 in qualified contract expenditures per year across an associated group (a maximum annual refundable credit of $4,000,000). Note that OBRITC (O. Reg. 37/09 s. 38) is the sole official statutory name of this credit.
5.3 Western Provinces: British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan, and Manitoba

In British Columbia (Sections 97 to 103, Income Tax Act [British Columbia] — Form T666), effective April 16, 2026, the provincial government repealed the former September 1, 2027 sunset clause to make the BC SR&ED Tax Credit permanent, and amended the statute to align with federal Bill C-15 by increasing the expenditure limit to $6,000,000 (phasing out between $15,000,000 and $75,000,000), reinstating capital expenditures after December 15, 2024, and expanding the 10% refundable credit (Schedule 5 Line 674) to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) alongside CCPCs for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024. Expenditures exceeding the $6,000,000 limit and expenditures of other corporations (or active corporate partners of partnerships) earn a 10% non-refundable credit (Schedule 5 Line 659), which carries back 3 years and carries forward 10 years (and may be renounced under Subsection 100(1)). Recapture applies if BC SR&ED property is sold or converted to commercial use within 10 years (Sections 102.1 to 102.6, Schedule 5 Line 241), and Form T666 must be filed within 18 months of tax year-end.

In Alberta (Sections 26.95 to 26.99, Alberta Corporate Tax Act — Form AT1 Schedule 29 [AT29] & Form AT4970), the Innovation Employment Grant (IEG) provides a 100% refundable grant delivered through the corporate tax system on up to $4,000,000 in annual Alberta SR&ED expenditures (matching federal SR&ED eligibility, including post-December 15, 2024 capital expenditures). The IEG pays an 8% base rate on eligible Alberta R&D spending up to the corporation's base level of spending (defined as the corporation's average qualifying Alberta R&D spending over the preceding 2 taxation years), and an enhanced 20% incremental rate on eligible spending that exceeds that two-year average base. The $4,000,000 maximum expenditure limit phases out incrementally for corporations (and associated groups) with prior-year taxable capital between $10,000,000 and $50,000,000 (eliminated at $50,000,000). Claims must be filed via AT1 Schedule 29 and Form AT4970 within 15 months after the AT1 filing-due date.

In Saskatchewan (Section 63.4, Income Tax Act, 2000 [Saskatchewan] — Schedule 403 [T2SCH403]), following the March 18, 2026 Saskatchewan Budget aligned with federal SR&ED expansion, the province doubled its 10% refundable CCPC expenditure limit from $1,000,000 to $2,000,000 per year (Schedule 5 Line 645, up to $200,000 refundable) and reinstated capital expenditures, retroactive to December 16, 2024 (taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024). Qualifying expenditures above the $2,000,000 CCPC threshold and qualifying expenditures of non-CCPCs earn a 10% non-refundable credit (Schedule 5 Line 631), subject to a combined annual cap of $1,000,000 in total refundable and non-refundable credits per corporation/associated group ($10,000,000 in qualifying spend). Unused non-refundable credits carry back 3 years, carry forward 10 years, and may be renounced under Subsection 63.4(13).

In Manitoba (Section 7.3, Income Tax Act [Manitoba] — Schedule 380 [T2SCH380]), corporations with a Manitoba permanent establishment earn a 15% tax credit on eligible Manitoba R&D expenditures (including current spend, capital expenditures on depreciable property other than buildings, and first/second-term SUE), with no expenditure limit. For in-house R&D, 50% of the credit is refundable (7.5% effective refundable rate, Schedule 5 Line 613) and 50% is non-refundable (7.5% effective non-refundable rate, Schedule 5 Line 606), whereas R&D conducted under an eligible contract with a qualifying research institute (e.g., Manitoba universities and colleges) is 100% refundable (full 15% refundable). Unused non-refundable credits carry back 3 years and carry forward 20 years, may be renounced under Subsection 7.3(7) (within 6 months of year-end for federal purposes), and Schedule 380 must be filed within 12 months after the T2 filing-due date.
5.4 Atlantic Provinces and Yukon Territory
Across Atlantic Canada and Yukon, four jurisdictions provide 100% refundable R&D tax credits with no upper expenditure limit:

items: Nova Scotia (Section 41, Income Tax Act [Nova Scotia] — Schedule 340 [T2SCH340]): 15% fully refundable tax credit (Schedule 5 Line 566) on eligible Nova Scotia SR&ED expenditures, available to all corporations (including corporate partners and trust beneficiaries) with a Nova Scotia permanent establishment. Subject to recapture (Schedule 5 Line 221), renunciation within 6 months of year-end (Subsection 41(7)), and an 18-month filing deadline after tax year-end.

New Brunswick (Section 59, New Brunswick Income Tax Act — Schedule 360 [T2SCH360]): 15% fully refundable tax credit (Schedule 5 Line 597) on eligible New Brunswick SR&ED expenditures for all corporations with a New Brunswick permanent establishment, subject to recapture (Schedule 5 Line 573).

Newfoundland and Labrador (Section 42, Income Tax Act, 2000 [Newfoundland and Labrador] — Schedule 301 [T2SCH301] / Form T1129): 15% fully refundable tax credit on eligible Newfoundland and Labrador SR&ED expenditures for corporations (Schedule 301), individuals, partnerships, and trusts (Form T1129), with no recapture and a 12-month filing deadline after the tax return filing-due date. Uniquely, Newfoundland and Labrador eligible expenditures are not reduced by government or non-government assistance (except GST/HST input tax credits), though the NL credit itself reduces federal qualified expenditures.

Yukon (Section 15, Income Tax Act [Yukon] — Schedule 442 [T2SCH442]): 15% fully refundable tax credit (Schedule 5 Line 698) on qualified Yukon SR&ED expenditures, plus an additional 5% (for a 20% total refundable credit) on amounts included above paid or payable to Yukon University, filed within 18 months of tax year-end.
