body.text: 6. Administrative Procedures, Pre-Claim Approval, Filing Deadlines, and Compliance Audits
6.1 The New Optional Pre-Claim Approval Process (Launched April 1, 2026 — Form T1322)

On April 1, 2026, the Canada Revenue Agency officially launched its Optional SR&ED Pre-Claim Approval Process, enabling eligible businesses to obtain a formal, upfront technical evaluation confirming that their planned or recently started R&D projects satisfy Subsection 248(1) before incurring significant costs or filing their annual tax return. To qualify for Pre-Claim Approval, the business must be a Canadian-controlled private corporation (CCPC), another Canadian corporation, or a Canadian partnership, have gross business income of less than $25,000,000, and be in good standing with the CRA. Furthermore, a claimant can request pre-claim approval for a maximum of 3 projects per application (Form T1322 Line 014), and the projects must not have been included in a prior SR&ED claim or involve issues under litigation.
The application follows a structured four-step workflow:

items: Request a Case Number: The business submits a five-minute online web form (Personal Information Bank CRA PPU 441). Existing SR&ED claimants in good standing receive a case number within 2 business days via My Business Account, while all other businesses are contacted within 5 business days by telephone.

Complete and Upload Form T1322: Using the case number (Line 016), the applicant completes Form T1322 (Application for Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Pre-Claim Approval) and uploads it via My Business Account along with Section D supporting documentation (project plans/Gantt charts, planned internal controls for tracking time and contemporaneous records, literature/patent due diligence references, and project team credentials). Section B of Form T1322 enforces strict word limits per project: Line 042 (maximum 500 words) requiring the scientific or technological uncertainty and objective; Line 043 (maximum 700 words) detailing the due diligence completed (literature, patents, standards, expert consultations, and preliminary trials) confirming existing knowledge cannot resolve the uncertainty; and Line 044 (maximum 900 words) describing the systematic investigation, hypotheses, experiments/analyses, and external contractors planned over the up-to-3-year period.

Technical Meeting with CRA Specialist (Within 4 Weeks): Within four weeks of submitting Form T1322, an assigned CRA Research and Technology Advisor (RTA) schedules a virtual meeting (typically lasting 2 to 5 hours) with the technical contact designated on Lines 028–032. This meeting is mandatory for new SR&ED claimants and conducted as needed for existing claimants in good standing.

Receive Official Determination (Within 8 Weeks) & 90-Day Expenditure Review: Within eight weeks of completing the application in My Business Account, the CRA issues its formal Pre-Claim Approval Evaluation Report. If granted, the pre-claim approval is valid for up to 3 years (though the claimant must still submit Form T661 and Schedule 31 annually after performing the work). For annual SR&ED claims containing pre-approved projects that require an expenditure review, the CRA's processing service standard is cut in half from 180 calendar days to 90 calendar days.

body.text: 6.2 Prescribed Post-Year-End Filing Forms and Statutory Deadlines (Subsections 37(11), 37(12), and 127(9)(m))

To access the Section 37 deduction and Section 127 ITC, every claimant must file prescribed forms containing all prescribed information on or before its SR&ED reporting deadline (SR&ED Filing Requirements Policy, updated January 28, 2025 & May 2026). The primary forms are Form T661 (Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Expenditures Claim, updated May 15, 2026) and Schedule T2SCH31 (Investment Tax Credit – Corporations, updated May 22, 2026) or Form T2038(IND) (Investment Tax Credit (Individuals) for sole proprietors and trusts). Where applicable, claimants must also file Schedule T2SCH49 (associated CCPC expenditure limit allocation, updated May 29, 2026, Subsection 127(10.3)), Form T1145 (NAL assistance allocation, updated May 15, 2026, Subsection 127(20)), Form T1146 (NAL contract qualified expenditure transfer, updated May 15, 2026, Subsection 127(13)), Form T1174 (associated corporation specified employee salary allocation, Subsection 37(9.2)), and Form T1263 (third-party payments).
The statutory SR&ED reporting deadline is strictly 12 months after the taxpayer's income tax return filing-due date:

items: Corporations (Form T2): Filing-due date is 6 months after tax year-end; SR&ED reporting deadline is 18 months after the end of the taxation year.

Individuals Carrying on a Business (Form T1): Filing-due date is June 15 of the following calendar year; SR&ED reporting deadline is June 15 of the subsequent year (17.5 months after a December 31 year-end).
Trusts (Form T3): Filing-due date is 90 days after the trust's tax year-end; SR&ED reporting deadline is 15 months after the trust's tax year-end.
Partnerships (Form T5013): Form T661 is filed with the T5013 partnership return, and each partner files Schedule 31 or Form T2038(IND) by their respective reporting deadline.

body.text: Under Subsections 37(11) and 37(12) and Paragraph 127(9)(m), the reporting deadline is an absolute statutory bar with no ministerial discretion for extension, and a "letter expressing intent to file" or unquantified estimate is invalid. If prescribed forms are filed after the reporting deadline, the expenditures are permanently precluded from being deducted as SR&ED or earning an ITC (Easyway Cattle, 2015 TCC 211; Westsource, 2017 TCC 9; Datacalc Research). However, under the CRA's Partial Disallowance Rule, if a claimant files Form T661 and Schedule 31 on time for multiple projects (e.g., 15 projects) but omits Part 2 technical project information for 5 of them, the CRA will not disallow the entire claim; the 10 complete projects will be accepted and only the 5 incomplete projects will be disallowed. Submitting claims at least 90 days prior to the reporting deadline (i.e., within 15 months of corporate year-end) allows the CRA to notify the claimant of any missing information before the deadline expires. Notably, deducting an existing Section 37 pool carryforward from a prior year, or providing Part 9 Claim Preparer Information, is not subject to the 18-month reporting deadline.
6.3 Claim Preparer Penalties (Subsections 162(5.1)–(5.3)) and Gross Negligence Penalties (Subsection 163(2))

Every Form T661 requires completion and certification of Part 9 – Claim Preparer Information, whether or not an external consultant assisted with the claim. Where a claim preparer accepted consideration to prepare or assist in preparing the claim, Part 9 requires the preparer's name, 15-character Business Number (or GST/HST number), Billing Arrangement Code (1 = Contingency fee arrangement, 2 = Hourly rate, 3 = Daily rate, 4 = Flat fee arrangement, 5 = Other arrangements), billing rate, and total fee paid, payable, or expected to be paid. Under Subsections 162(5.1), 162(5.2), and 162(5.3) of the Income Tax Act, if prescribed claim preparer information is missing, incomplete, or inaccurate, a $1,000 penalty may be assessed per SR&ED claim, for which the claimant and the claim preparer are jointly and severally (or solidarily) liable.

Under the Gross Negligence Penalty on Overstated SR&ED Claims Policy (updated January 28, 2025) and Subsection 163(2) of the Income Tax Act, any person who knowingly, or under circumstances amounting to gross negligence, makes or participates in a false statement or omission in an original or amended SR&ED claim is liable to a penalty equal to the greater of $100 or 50% of the understated Part I tax payable and/or the overstated refundable ITC claimed. For penalty calculation purposes, the CRA treats overstated amounts as being deducted first before valid amounts, and subsequent taxpayer requests to offset disallowed SR&ED deductions with Capital Cost Allowance do not reduce the penalty. As demonstrated in Les Éléments Chauffants Tempora Inc. v. The King (2025 TCC 173) and criminal fraud prosecutions (R. v. Elhami, 2017 QCCQ 2684; Tempora, SCC 2018), plagiarized or fabricated technical narratives reopen statute-barred years and result in civil penalties and, on conviction, criminal fines of 50% to 200% (100% to 200% on indictment) of the overstated refund or credit claimed (Subsections 239(1.1) and 239(2)).
6.4 CRA Review Process, Dispute Resolution, and Administrative Review (Form RC532)

Under The SR&ED Review Process: A Guide for Claimants (updated July 2, 2025 / April 20, 2026) and the Guidelines for Resolving Claimants' SR&ED Concerns (updated December 5, 2025), the CRA aims to process refundable SR&ED claims within 180 calendar days of receiving a complete claim (90 calendar days for expenditure-only reviews of pre-approved projects). Once a claim is selected for review, it cannot be withdrawn because Form T661 is a certified part of the tax return. Reviews are conducted predominantly via virtual videoconferencing by a Research and Technology Advisor (RTA) (evaluating Subsection 248(1) work eligibility) and a Financial Reviewer (FR) (auditing expenditure calculations). Under the Claim Review Manual for Research and Technology Advisors, RTAs are strictly prohibited from negotiating eligibility or trading off projects, though they may work with the FR and claimant to establish a reasonable basis for an expenditure estimate where SR&ED performance is proven. Also, under Application Policy SR&ED 95-04R (Conflict of Interest with Regard to Outside Consultants), outside technical consultants retained by the CRA must declare any conflict of interest and provide their CV to the taxpayer upon request.
If disagreements arise during a review, the CRA provides a four-step escalation pathway before and after assessment:

items: Step 1 — Direct Discussion with Reviewers: Discussing technical or financial findings directly with the RTA and/or FR;
Step 2 — Involving Managers: Escalating unresolved issues to the Research and Technology Manager (RTM) and/or Financial Review Manager (FRM);

Step 3 — Requesting an Administrative Review (Form RC532): After receiving the CRA Proposal Package and before the 30-day proposal period expires (prior to file closure), the claimant may submit Form RC532 (Request for Administrative Review) to the National SR&ED Administrative Review Intake Centre (Business Tax Incentives Directorate, Enterprise Building, 13th Floor, 427 Laurier Ave W, Ottawa ON K1A 0L5), which forwards it within 3 business days to the local SR&ED Assistant Director to evaluate whether due process was provided and whether the review complied with legislation and policy; and

Step 4 — Formal Notice of Objection & Tax Court Appeal: Filing a formal Notice of Objection with the CRA Appeals Branch within 90 days of the Notice of Assessment/Reassessment, followed by an appeal to the Tax Court of Canada (Section 169).

body.text: 7. Judicial Precedents and Case Law Analysis (1988–2026)
7.1 The Five-Question Legal Test: Northwest Hydraulic Consultants, CW Agencies, Sass Manufacturing, and RIS-Christie

The foundational common-law test for determining whether an activity constitutes SR&ED under Subsection 248(1) was established by Justice Donald Bowman in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen, 98 DTC 1839, [1998] 3 C.T.C. 2520 (TCC), and summarized into five sequential questions by the Federal Court of Appeal in C.W. Agencies Inc. v. Canada, 2001 FCA 393, 2002 DTC 6740 (FCA):

items: Technological Risk or Uncertainty: Was there a technological risk or uncertainty, which could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures? Routine engineering refers to techniques, procedures, and data generally accessible to competent professionals in the field. Uncertainty includes system uncertainty, which arises when known components or open-source tools interact in a complex system in ways that cannot be predicted or resolved by standard engineering practice (Northwest Hydraulic; Buhler Versatile Inc. v. The King, 2023 TCC 18; Dazzm Inc. v. The King, 2024 TCC 129; Willowglen Systems Inc. v. The King, 2026 TCC 7).

Formulation of Hypotheses: Did the person claiming to be doing SR&ED formulate hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty? This requires a five-stage methodology: (a) observing the subject matter of the problem; (b) formulating a clear objective; (c) identifying and articulating the technological uncertainty; (d) formulating a hypothesis or hypotheses designed to reduce or eliminate the uncertainty; and (e) methodical and systematic testing of the hypotheses. Merely identifying a problem without formulating and testing causal hypotheses is not SR&ED (Indusol Industrial Control, 2020 TCC 103).

Adherence to the Scientific Method: Did the procedure adopted accord with the total discipline of the scientific method including the formulation, testing, and modification of hypotheses? As established in Sass Manufacturing Limited v. M.N.R., 88 DTC 1363 (TCC) and RIS-Christie Ltd. v. The Queen, 99 DTC 5087 (FCA), systematic investigation requires trained observation, measurement, repeatable experimentation or analysis, and iterative modification of hypotheses based on test results, rather than intuitive trial and error.

Technological Advancement: Did the process result in a technological advancement? As held in Northwest Hydraulic, Rainbow Pipe Line Co. v. The Queen (99 DTC 1081 (TCC)), and Canafric Inc. v. The King (2023 TCC), commercial failure or the rejection of a hypothesis is itself a technological advancement if it generates new knowledge eliminating an avenue of uncertainty for competent professionals in the field.

Detailed Contemporaneous Records: Was a detailed record of the hypotheses tested, and results kept as the work progressed? While the Income Tax Act does not make written documentation an absolute statutory prerequisite where credible, detailed oral testimony bridges specific documentary gaps (Canafric Inc. v. The King, 2023 TCC; Les Abeilles Service de Conditionnement Inc. v. The Queen, 2014 TCC 313), the absence of contemporaneous experimental records is fatal whenever oral accounts fail to establish systematic hypothesis testing (RIS-Christie; Vortex Energy Services, 2025 TCC 63; Tuna Temple Inc. v. Canada, 2026 FCA 175).

body.text: 7.2 Appellate Alignment with CRA's "Why" and "How" Guidelines: Kam-Press (2021 FCA 88) and National R&D (2022 FCA 72)

In August 2021, the CRA replaced its archived Eligibility of Work Policy with the Guidelines on the Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Tax Incentives, framing eligibility around two core requirements: the "Why" Requirement (why the work is conducted—scientific or technological uncertainty and targeted advancement, corresponding to Northwest Hydraulic Questions 1 and 4) and the "How" Requirement (how the work is conducted—systematic investigation via hypothesis generation, testing by experiment/analysis, logical conclusions, and contemporaneous record-keeping, corresponding to Questions 2, 3, and 5).

In National R&D Inc. v. Canada, 2022 FCA 72 (affirming 2020 TCC 47) and Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. Canada, 2021 FCA 88, the Federal Court of Appeal rejected taxpayer arguments that the scientific method criterion had no statutory basis in Subsection 248(1) or had been relaxed by the CRA's August 2021 guidelines. The FCA held that the five Northwest Hydraulic criteria remain the binding legal test across both natural and applied sciences, that the CRA's "How" requirement preserves the exact same demand for experimental rigour and discipline, and that a proposed expert witness whose report was 65% written by the taxpayer's president and opined on the ultimate legal question of SR&ED eligibility was properly disqualified for lack of impartiality.
7.3 Recent Jurisprudence (2023–2026): Canafric, Dazzm, Willowglen Systems, and Tuna Temple (2026 FCA 175)
Between 2023 and November 2026, Canadian courts issued four pivotal decisions defining the boundaries of SR&ED eligibility and evidentiary proof:

items: Canafric Inc. v. The King (2023 TCC): The Tax Court upheld $343,449 in SR&ED expenditures and $60,963 in ITCs across the 2013–2016 taxation years for a frozen-pie manufacturer developing preservative-free, extended-shelf-life, antibiotic-free, and structural-integrity formulations. The Court ruled that systematic formulation hypotheses, taste/stability panels, and root-cause analysis of failed recipes satisfied all five Northwest Hydraulic criteria, and that detailed, factual oral testimony from the CEO cured gaps in written documentation.

Dazzm Inc. v. The King (2024 TCC 129): The Tax Court allowed a software engineering appeal involving cloud-based SaaS integration and React/Redux performance bottlenecks, holding that resolving systemic uncertainty in integrating open-source tools went beyond routine debugging or standard optimization and endorsing a holistic evaluation of software projects supported by metrics and testimony.

Willowglen Systems Inc. v. The King (2026 TCC 7): In a split decision on industrial control software, the Tax Court allowed the MTCLM (SIL 4 train-control box) project based on cumulative system uncertainty not resolvable by available methods, but disallowed $1,293,692 on the SCADACOM-5 upgrade because modernizing and scaling up software with known tools is commercial product development, not experimental development.

Tuna Temple Inc. v. Canada (2026 FCA 175, decided October 21, 2026; affirming 2025 TCC 183): In this landmark October 2026 appellate ruling, the Federal Court of Appeal upheld the disallowance of 13 of 14 food-processing and recipe projects (2005–2009). The taxpayer argued that because the Tax Court judge had found its sole witness credible, and the Crown had neither displaced his testimony on cross-examination nor called a witness to contradict it, the taxpayer must win. The FCA unanimously dismissed the appeal with costs, holding that believing a witness is honest (credibility) is legally distinct from finding that the evidence establishes a prima facie case demolishing the Minister's assumptions (sufficiency). Because the witness's credible testimony described trial-and-error batch adjustments rather than systematic hypothesis testing, failed to establish an industry-wide knowledge gap, lacked experimental records, and relied on wages estimated and split evenly across batches, the claim failed the Northwest Hydraulic test.

body.text: 8. Step-by-Step Compliance Playbook for Canadian R&D Claimants

To maximize combined federal and provincial recovery while insulating claims against CRA technical and financial audit adjustments, Canadian corporations and tax practitioners should execute the following six-stage compliance protocol:

items: Evaluate Pre-Claim Approval Eligibility Before Commencing Major Projects: For CCPC, ECPC, or partnership claimants with under $25,000,000 in gross business income embarking on new R&D initiatives, submit a case number request and file Form T1322 via My Business Account to secure a three-year Pre-Claim Approval determination within eight weeks and halve post-filing expenditure review timelines from 180 days to 90 days.

Structure Project Boundaries Around Technological Uncertainty, Not Commercial Products: Following Willowglen Systems (2026 TCC 7) and Dazzm (2024 TCC 129), carve out the specific subsystem or architectural integration where standard engineering practice failed (Line 242 / Line 042), document the literature/benchmark due diligence proving a genuine knowledge gap (Line 043), and exclude routine commercial scaling, UI/UX styling, and post-resolution production runs.

Maintain Contemporaneous Evidence Linking Hypotheses, Iterations, and Time Allocation: As underscored by Tuna Temple Inc. v. Canada (2026 FCA 175), honest retrospective testimony cannot substitute for contemporaneous records. Link Git commits, Jira/Azure DevOps tickets, lab logs, test failure metrics, and scrap records directly to specific hypotheses, and maintain contemporaneous bi-weekly or monthly time-tracking logs rather than year-end percentage estimates.

Model Proxy vs. Traditional Overhead and Capital Spend Post-December 15, 2024: Compare the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (Regulation 2900(4)) against actual tracked overhead (Line 360), factoring in cloud computing/SaaS costs (which are double-counted and disallowed under the Proxy Method), specified employee 2.5 × YMPE ($186,500 in 2026) and 75% time caps, the Regulation 2900(6) Overall PPA Cap (A − B − C), and reinstated post-December 15, 2024 capital expenditures (Line 390), Shared-Use Equipment (Line 504), and lease costs (Line 350/360).

Optimize Provincial Credit Stacking and Waivers/Renunciations: In Québec, map both R&D and pre-commercialization (regulatory validation, certification testing, product design) and capital equipment into the new 30%/20% refundable CRIC (Form RD-1029.8.CR-T) while ensuring no double-claiming with C3i or CDAE-IA. In Ontario, British Columbia, Saskatchewan, and Manitoba, evaluate whether non-refundable provincial credit tiers (e.g., the 3.5% Ontario ORDTC) should be waived or renounced within six months of year-end if the corporation is in a multi-year tax loss position, so that non-cash provincial credits do not erode the 35% fully refundable federal SR&ED ITC base.

Enforce Strict 180-Day Payment Cutoffs and 15/18-Month Filing Calendars: Verify that all accrued SR&ED bonuses (for non-specified employees), salaries (Subsection 78(4)), and subcontractor/material payables (Subsection 127(26)) are disbursed within 180 days of fiscal year-end, file all associated group and non-arm's length agreements (Schedule 49, Form T1145, Form T1146, Form T1174), complete Form T661 Part 9 accurately to avoid the $1,000 Subsection 162(5.1) penalty, and transmit the complete T661 and Schedule 31 package at least 90 days prior to the absolute 18-month statutory deadline.
